extracted.intended_audience: writers of historical fiction (and fiction writers seeking to create immersive settings)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for creating immersive, character-rooted settings in historical fiction (applicable to any fiction). Focuses on sensory detail, perspective-filtered description, setting-as-character, setting-driven plot, and macro/micro level choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting is a collection of details—narrow the focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is a collection of details—the right details in the right amount. Immersive setting is not about expanding; it is about narrowing. Narrow the reader’s focus on what matters most and the place will come alive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Curate the essential elements of the characters’ surroundings for the reader rather than dumping everything you know. Only include what moves your story forward; less is more. Avoid including every archival fact you unearth—select details that serve character, mood, or plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop vivid sensory details
rubrics_metrics.description: Call on all of your characters’ senses. Challenge yourself to include senses other than sight so description feels fresh and immersive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid clichés and overused phrases (examples given: “The wail of the siren,” “The warm flush in her cheeks,” “The fresh pine”). Exercise: close your eyes and imagine you’re in the scene (e.g., 1924 Paris or 1898 Puerto Rico); ask what you would be smelling, hearing, tasting or touching and what one element would stand out to your character. Make that specific, character-relevant sensory anchor the focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal character emotions through place (filter description through perspective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting is personal; description should be filtered through your character’s perspective rather than reading like a guidebook or the author’s travel notes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider your character’s emotional state and relationship to the location. Use different perspectives to change mood and word choice (e.g., a noble vs. a lady-in-waiting vs. a peasant). Ask how the narrator’s diction and focus would differ and let that reveal emotion rather than telling it directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a setting that acts as a character (give setting a past)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every place, like every character, has a past which informs its present. A setting with a sense of history can feel like a personality rather than an untethered backdrop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore the setting’s backstory—but don’t include pages of irrelevant history. Consider how the location’s past has affected your character socially or personally, whether it forces decisions, and how you can use the setting’s history to target conflict in the present. (Author warns: don’t be afraid to use the “B-word” — backstory — judiciously.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Make setting a catalyst for characters’ actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dynamic settings cause change; if something in the environment changes it can force characters to act and drive the story forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural disasters, social shifts, or smaller alterations (add or remove an important element) to prompt choices and conflict. Example: a 1935 hurricane touches every character and forces choices; smaller devices (e.g., park statues that are cameras, a town-wide power outage) can similarly compel action. The setting should actively move the story rather than merely decorate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utilize macro and micro setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Settings operate at two levels: macro (the overarching historical/place label that evokes a reader response) and micro (sentence-level word choice and sensory images).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Macro examples: 'China 1949', 'Boston 1776', 'The Dust Bowl'—these labels bring cultural/emotional resonance. Micro choices (e.g., whether snow is 'blustery' or 'delightful', whether pearls feel 'nostalgic' or a 'burden') determine tone and perception through the character’s lens. Research (archives, primary sources, photo collections such as NYPL Digital Collections) to ground choices, but apply 'less is more'—only include details that advance story, character, or conflict.
